title: Sequential Probabilistic Uncertainty Estimation for Parallel Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems
claim: Final answers hide reliability differences; stable versus oscillating interaction dynamics need a sequential belief update to estimate uncertainty.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; left shows stable vs unstable rows, right shows stacked update stages
description: The figure has two boxed panels. Panel A (green header, 'Problem: uncertainty is about interaction dynamics') shows two rows of three rounds of agent icons, each giving answers A, B or C in small bubbles. The top stable row converges to A and ends in a green 'low uncertainty' box. The bottom unstable row oscillates and ends in a red 'high uncertainty' box, though its final answer is also A. Below, a gray 'static view' box shows agents summed into a single uncertainty, with a red X for 'cannot distinguish'. An arrow leads to a blue 'Need: uncertainty from multi-round dynamics' box. Panel B (blue header, 'SAUCE: dynamic uncertainty update') stacks three-round agent outputs, then observations M_t and R_t. Below them are a latent chain v0 to v3 ('reliability weighted') and a belief chain mu0 to mu3. A purple box gives the SAUCE score u(x,τ) as the negative mean of mu_t.
caption: Overview. (A) Two MAS trajectories can reach the same final answer but differ greatly in reliability: a stable run whose outputs converge across rounds (top) is more trustworthy than an unstable run whose outputs oscillate (bottom). A static view that only considers the final output cannot distinguish them, motivating uncertainty estimation from interaction dynamics. (B) \ours models multi-round interaction as a sequence of round-level observations $(M_t, R_t)$, where agreement is weighted by generation uncertainty, and performs a filtering-style update over a latent system-level belief. The resulting trajectory summary defines the \ours uncertainty score $u(\vx,\tau)$ (\Eqref{eq:final-u}).
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.
